title: Diagnosing Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease in a Patient with a Suspected Status Epilepticus in the Intensive Care Unit
case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman with a history of postnatal depression and hysterectomy presented with a one-month history of aberrant emotional behavior and, over the subsequent 17 days, developed derealization, gait instability, and visual hallucinations.  
Initial head CT and brain MRI were interpreted as normal. Five days later, she became increasingly confused, psychotic, and catatonic and was admitted to the psychiatric ward.  
Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with normal cell counts and no intrathecal IgG production. During her psychiatric admission, minor shoulder myoclonus and worsening consciousness prompted transfer to neurology one week later.  
Electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrated diffuse slowing with periodic and semiperiodic sharp-wave complexes that were transiently attenuated by intravenous clonazepam; on continuous EEG monitoring, these complexes recurred at approximately 1-second intervals despite treatment with clonazepam, lorazepam, and valproic acid.  
Repeat brain MRI showed symmetrical T2, FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted hyperintensities in the caudate nuclei and putamina, with less pronounced cortical and pulvinar signal changes. Repeat CSF analysis remained normal.  
Extensive infectious studies—including Borrelia, Coxiella, Whipple, syphilis, Bartonella, Mycoplasma, Herpes Simplex virus, Varicella Zoster virus, measles, enteroviruses, and parechoviruses—were negative.  
CSF testing for anti–N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor, anti-Hu, anti–voltage-gated potassium channel, and anti–glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies was negative.  
A toxicology screen, vitamin B6 and B12 levels, thyroid function tests, antinuclear and antiphospholipid antibodies, and urine porphyrins were normal or negative.  
Empiric intravenous immunoglobulins and corticosteroids for suspected anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis produced no clinical improvement.  
She subsequently developed recurrent myoclonus, left-arm dyskinesia, and nonresponsiveness, requiring induction of a burst-suppression coma with midazolam and thiopental.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Autoimmune (anti-NMDA) encephalitis was considered given her psychosis and catatonia but was not supported by response to immunotherapy — “pragmatic treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins and steroids for suspected anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis were administered, however, without any improvement.”  
2. Infectious encephalitis was excluded after an extensive panel of neurotrophic pathogens tested negative — “a variety of possible neurotrophic infectious agents, including Borrelia, Coxiella, Whipple, Syphilis, Bartonella, Mycoplasma, and Herpes Simplex-, Varicella Zoster-, Measles-, Entero-, and Parechoviruses were investigated, which were all negative.”  
3. Paraneoplastic and other autoimmune causes were ruled out by negative CSF antibody testing — “Earlier requested CSF analysis revealed no anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, and the other paraneoplastic/autoimmune antibodies were also absent.”  
4. Toxic and metabolic encephalopathies were excluded based on normal toxicology, vitamin levels, thyroid function, and autoimmune serologies — “A general toxicological screening was performed, which revealed no substance abuse and no plasma heavy metals. Vitamin levels (B6, B12) were normal. Thyroid disease was ruled out and autoimmune serology…was negative.”  
5. Refractory nonconvulsive status epilepticus was considered due to persistent periodic sharp-wave complexes but remained unresponsive to adequate antiepileptic therapy and anesthetic coma — “Despite antiepileptic drugs being in therapeutic ranges and addition of levetiracetam, the burst-suppression pattern was difficult to realize.”
